en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on the Pairs, 30. The Training Rule on What Has Been Consumed.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a certain guild in Sāvatthī had prepared a meal together with robes for the Saṅgha, thinking,
"Having fed them, we shall clothe them with robes.
Then the group-of-six monks approached that guild.
Having approached, they said this to that group:
"Friends, give us these robes.
"We will not give them, venerable sirs."
“An annual alms-offering of robes has been established for our Saṅgha.
“There are many donors for the Saṅgha, friend; there are many supporters of the Saṅgha.
It is by depending on you and looking to you that we dwell here.”
"If you do not give these to us, who indeed will give them to us? Give us these robes, friends!
Then that group, being pressured by the Group-of-Six monks, gave the robes as they had been prepared to the Group-of-Six monks and served a meal to the Saṅgha.
Those monks who knew that a meal with robes had been prepared for the Saṅgha, but did not know that it had been given to the group of six monks, said:
“Please serve the robes to the Saṅgha, friends. [The others replied:
“There are none, Venerable Sirs.”
“The group-of-six noble ladies have diverted to themselves the robe that was prepared for them.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can the group-of-six monks, knowing that a gain intended for the Saṅgha has been diverted, divert it to themselves?”
Then those monks, having rebuked the group-of-six monks in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“… ‘Is it true, monks, that you knowingly diverted to yourselves material gain that had been dedicated to the Saṅgha?’—
‘It is true, Blessed One.’”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“…How, you foolish men, can you knowingly divert to yourselves a gain that has been dedicated to the Saṅgha?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“Whosoever, a monk, knowingly diverts to himself a gain that has been assigned to the Saṅgha, there is an offense of expiation involving relinquishment.
Whosoever, it is said:
Whoever is such a one … [as described] … “a bhikkhu” … [and so on] … this is the meaning intended here by the term “bhikkhu.”
"Knows" means either he knows it himself, or others inform him of it, or he informs [the Sangha] himself.
"Belonging to the Sangha" means:
It has been given to the Saṅgha and relinquished.
"Gain" refers to robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; even down to a lump of powder, a tooth-stick, or a thread for a fringe.
"Appropriated" means that the speech has been broken by saying, "We shall give," or "We shall do.
If one appropriates it for oneself, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the act of application.
By the very act of receiving it, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya).
It must be relinquished to either the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
And this, monks, is how it should be relinquished.
…pe… “Venerable sir, this gain belonging to the Saṅgha which I knowingly diverted for myself—
I relinquish it to the Saṅgha as something to be forfeited. …pe…
"Should give" means...
"should give" means...
"I give to the Venerable One."
If it has been dedicated, and he perceives it as dedicated, and he dedicates it to himself, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If it has been dedicated, but he is unsure of it, and he dedicates it to himself, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it has been dedicated, but he perceives it as not dedicated, and he dedicates it to himself, there is no offense.
If one diverts what has been dedicated to the Saṅgha to another Saṅgha, or to a shrine (cetiyassa), there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one diverts what has been dedicated to a shrine to another shrine, or to the Saṅgha, or to an individual (puggala), there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one diverts what has been dedicated to an individual to another individual, or to the Saṅgha, or to a shrine, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is not yet digested, but he perceives it as digested, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is not yet digested, but he is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is not yet digested, and he perceives it as not yet digested, there is no offense.

There is no offense if, when asked, "Where should we give? one says: "Give it where your gift may be used, or where it may be restored, or where it will endure for a long time; or else, give it wherever your heart feels confident."
"In the case of one who is insane,
and in the case of the first offender.
The tenth training rule concerning what has been transformed is finished.
The Third Chapter on Bowls.
Its summary:
Two bowls and medicine.
The *vassikā* flower, the fifth being the gift;
one who weaves it himself, one who has it woven by another,
that which is suspicious, and that which belongs to the Saṅgha.
“Venerable sirs, the thirty rules on offenses entailing relinquishment and confession have been recited.
In this regard, I ask the venerable ones:
‘Are you pure in this matter?’”
A second time I ask:
“Are you pure in this matter? A third time I ask: “Are you pure in this matter?”
‘Are you pure in this matter?
‘The Venerable Ones are pure in this matter; therefore they are silent.
Thus do I understand it.’
The Section on Forfeiture is finished.
The Pārājika Canon is finished.
